abstract: This paper examines how Türkiye can operationalize the policy direction established by the 2023 amendment to the Natural Gas Market Law through a hybrid institutional architecture that reconciles strategic procurement, targeted household protection, private participation, and competitive domestic gas trading. The post-2023 decline in Organized Wholesale Natural Gas Market (OTSP) activity underscores the gap between legislative reform and market implementation. Building on institutional path dependence, second-best institutional design, and Türkiye’s social-state tradition, the study develops a Dual-Ring architecture comprising a Guardian Ring for supported household demand and a Competitive Ring for market-exposed volumes. It complements this structure with AggregateTR, a variable-intensity strategic procurement mechanism, and two Structural Market Indicators: the Support Signal Distortion Index (SSDI) and the Traded Volume Ratio (TVR). A 2023 empirical baseline anchors SSDI and TVR in observed household support and OTSP activity. The framework is evaluated through three stylized 2030 scenarios that vary household-support allocation, competitive use of Sakarya gas production, OTSP traded volumes, private participation, spot LNG exposure, and the gas-on-gas competition (GOG)/oil-price escalation (OPE) balance, together with a demand sensitivity analysis. The scenarios indicate that better-targeted household support, competitive allocation of domestic gas, higher organized-market activity, and diversified procurement can strengthen the conditions for market-based price formation while preserving affordability and supply-security objectives. The paper concludes that Türkiye’s 2023 reform direction can be implemented through an adaptive hybrid architecture rather than full liberalization and recommends a National Natural Gas Strategy Paper to guide implementation through 2030 and beyond.
title: Türkiye’s gas market reform: A hybrid institutional pathway for competition and resilience

abstract: This survey reviews approaches to measuring indirect labour market effects of policies and shocks. Fixed‐price multipliers organize gross supply‐chain and expenditure linkages, but do not generally measure net job creation. Regional exposure and quasi‐experimental designs provide credible evidence on local responses, but usually identify relative local effects rather than aggregate incidence. Spatial and sectoral general equilibrium models can trace spillovers, displacement, and welfare effects, but require empirical discipline. Recent work on trade shocks, fiscal multipliers, procurement, and place‐based policy shows the value of combining regional exposure evidence with spatial general equilibrium structure. The survey draws implications for Canadian policy evaluation.
title: Indirect labour market impacts: Spillovers, displacement and policy evaluation

abstract: We study the relationship between local crime and residents’ charitable donations and explore the mechanisms underlying this relationship. The analysis combines longitudinal postcode-level data on charitable donations made through a UK giving portal with publicly available data on local crime and neighbourhood characteristics. Our main results suggest that an increase in local crime corresponds to a significant rise in the size of unscheduled charitable donations. This pattern is primarily driven by the donation choices of female and gender-unclassified donors. The strength of the relationship between local crime and donation amounts also varies with postcode-specific population characteristics, such as religiosity, age, and mental health.
title: Local Crime and Prosocial Behaviours: Evidence from Charitable Donations

abstract: This study examines whether racial outrage in the media can result from the incentives of elites who seek to divide society for political gain, focusing on the late 19th century Southern United States. At this time, the Democratic Party had strong political incentives to incite racial outrage, and local Democratic elites exercised considerable influence over newspapers, the only mass media at the time. Using high-frequency historical newspaper data and difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimation strategies, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign to sway white voters. Supporting analyses are consistent with Democrats benefiting from anti-Black propaganda in the subsequent elections.
journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
title: The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from US Newspapers,

abstract: This paper studies how lifetime inflation exposure shapes individuals’ inflation expectations, perceptions, and financial behavior. Using a large individual-level dataset from Türkiye spanning 2014 to 2024, combined with detailed measures of past inflation experiences, we show that individuals who have lived through higher inflation consistently report higher expected and perceived inflation. They also respond more strongly to current inflation conditions. The effects are larger for less educated and lower income individuals. In additional analysis, we find that greater lifetime inflation exposure is associated with higher use of retail loans, especially fixed rate loans. These results highlight the persistent influence of past economic conditions on expectation formation and household decisions in an emerging economy with a history of volatile inflation.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 252
title: Echoes of hyperinflation: The link between past exposure and formation of expectations

abstract: We evaluate the enforcement of China Walls—information barriers within conglomerates. We focus on July 2018, when the SEC tightened enforcement around broker-dealer subsidiaries, and on the 25 million Israeli Shekel trades over 2018–2024. Our difference-in-differences design compares a dealer’s affiliate, connected, and unrelated funds on days when the dealer likely obtained valuable information. Before July 2018, dealers share information with their affiliate and connected funds. After July 2018: the sharing ceases only with the affiliate funds; price discovery slows; trading costs fall for affiliate funds and rise for other funds. Tightly enforced walls eliminated 99.0% of affiliate funds’ event-day profits.

abstract: We develop a “hardware–software” framework for analysing production, technological change, and economic growth. Grounded in first principles, it distinguishes energy inputs, supplied by hardware (human physical labour, physical capital, and computing infrastructure), from information inputs, supplied by software (human cognitive work and digital technologies, including artificial intelligence). Hardware and software are essential, complementary inputs to production. The framework generalises neoclassical production models, incorporates capital–skill complementarity and skill-biased technical change, and extends selected unified growth frameworks. Using US data for 1968–2019, we document rising shares of physical capital within hardware, reflecting mechanisation, and digital software within software, reflecting automation. Software has grown systematically faster than hardware. Human capital and digital software emerge as key contributors to economic growth. The framework also enables analysis of alternative growth scenarios, including full automation through transformative AI and potentially accelerated economic growth. These findings advance growth theory and inform policy debates on the economic implications of rapidly advancing AI capabilities.
title: Hardware and software: A new perspective on the past and future of economic growth

abstract: This paper examines how green finance affects employment stability through energy-sector adjustment. Evidence from China’s 2012 Green Credit Guidelines is combined with firm-level tax-survey data, China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) household data, and a heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model with career-stage heterogeneity. The firm-level estimates show that the policy reduced affected firms’ reliance on brown-energy inputs and compressed short-run labor demand. A separate CFPS analysis of workers in production- and transport-related occupations indicates that adverse employment effects are concentrated among late-career workers, and this qualitative pattern is robust to an age-bin specification. Because the tax-survey and CFPS samples are not linked at the worker or firm level, the CFPS estimates provide complementary evidence on worker-side incidence rather than a direct decomposition of the firm-level labor-demand decline. In the model, late-career vulnerability reflects skill mismatch and sector-specific human capital, whereas early-career workers primarily experience temporary frictional unemployment. The model further shows that unemployment insurance (UI) can smooth liquidity constraints and reduce transition-related employment volatility; lifelong vocational skills training is more effective in reducing structural unemployment among late-career workers; and fiscal employment support can raise labor demand in the short run but may slow the green transition when brown-energy sectors absorb additional demand. These findings suggest implementing green finance alongside targeted UI, career-stage-specific retraining, and environmentally guided employment support.

title: Green Finance, Energy Transition and Employment Stability across Career Stages: Evidence from China’s Green Credit Policy and a Heterogeneous-Agent Model

abstract: We develop a model of electoral competition that captures the dynamic interaction between the incumbent’s policy making and the informed opposition’s response. An incumbent has an opportunity to introduce a reform. If the incumbent introduces the reform, the opposition can either acquiesce to it or promise to repeal it. Parties know whether the reform is partisan or common interest, but the voter does not. The voter observes the parties’ decisions and decides which party to elect for the next period. We show that parties’ platforms converge on the choice that is best for the voter only if common-interest reforms are sufficiently valuable, the incumbent is strongly office motivated, and the opposition is not. When these conditions fail, the opposition commits to policy repeal even when the incumbent’s reform is common interest. Such inefficient repeals induce the incumbent to either forego common-interest reforms (gridlock) or double down on partisan reforms (policy divergence). In the latter case, some common-interest reforms are introduced, but then are subsequently repealed with positive probability, while some of the partisan reforms survive.
title: Policy Making with an Informed Opposition

abstract: This paper examines the unintended corporate costs of sanctions in the sanctioning country arising from its geoeconomic dependence on the sanction target, focusing on the EU–Russia conflict following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Exploiting changes in the variance–covariance structure of financial and news variables with gas prices on official sanction and countersanction announcement days, the paper develops a novel measure of sanction intensity. Sanction intensity raises credit spreads in the sanction-imposing countries by 8% at the start of the full-scale invasion, with effects around 30% stronger for firms highly dependent on Russia before the war. After 100 days, the increase in spreads is equally split between elevated fundamental default risk and a higher excess bond premium. The financial cost of sanction intensity spills over to the real economy as corporate investment declines, primarily due to higher borrowing costs, while bankruptcies rise due to gas price responses.
title: The price of geoeconomic dependence: Sanction intensity and corporate credit spreads

abstract: Why did the same conflict move energy prices so differently across countries? Following the Russia-Ukraine war, a recent factor-augmented vector autoregression study finds that some economies absorbed the shock directly, others mainly through the world oil price, others through their own currency, and a fourth group barely moved at all. This paper builds a small structural model that explains why. Four country-level parameters–direct exposure to conflict-zone infrastructure, integration into global energy and activity markets, exchange-rate pass-through, and fiscal-buffering intensity–map in closed form onto the four reduced-form transmission channels the empirical study estimates. Four propositions show, respectively, when each parameter dominates a country’s energy-price variance, reproducing the four empirical archetypes: directly exposed European economies, global integrators, currency-unstable economies, and administratively priced exporters. A corollary shows that the empirical insensitivity of the results to the ordering of shocks follows directly from the low correlation between the conflict shock and other global aggregates. I calibrate the model to nine representative countries, matching the sign and broad magnitude of their empirical responses, and derive a policy-relevant exposure-versus-buffering typology. The results clarify which diversification, fiscal, and exchange-rate policies are best suited to containing future geopolitical energy shocks in each type of economy.
title: The heterogeneous transmission of geopolitical energy shocks: A structural framework

abstract: As sustainability claims proliferate on food packaging, understanding their implicit market value is important for effective policy design and competitive firm strategy. This study quantifies the price premiums of sustainability attributes in the U.S. market using product‐level data. We analyze 210,515 food and beverage product launches from the Mintel Global New Products Database (2012–2024) and document a near‐doubling in the prevalence of sustainability claims, rising from 18% of new products in 2012 to 37% in 2024. Using a hedonic price model, we present significant price premiums for both environmental (7.9%) and social (3.5%) claims. Further decomposition reveals substantial heterogeneity, with “downstream” attributes related to disposal (e.g., biodegradable) generating the highest premiums, outperforming “upstream” production claims. Additionally, premiums vary widely across product categories, with large premiums in beverages, but zero or negative premiums in several utilitarian categories such as Sauces and Seasonings. These findings inform ongoing policy discussions on third‐party certification, standardized claim definitions, and disclosure requirements for sustainability claims.
title: Price Premiums for Sustainability Claims: Evidence From U.S. Food and Beverage Markets

abstract: Using 23,908 person-year observations from the 2016–2022 China Family Panel Studies, this article presents a correlational analysis of perceived income position and job satisfaction among Chinese wage workers. Perceived rank is a five-point assessment of personal income in the local area; measured rank is the county-year quintile of annual work income. Their difference defines a descriptive rank gap. The main outcome averages satisfaction with work safety, the work environment and working time. A one-point higher gap is associated with 0.047 points higher non-pay job satisfaction. Conditional on income ventiles and measured-rank indicators, the perceived-rank coefficient is 0.140 in the pooled model and 0.076 with person fixed effects. Joint adjustment for general evaluation, job characteristics and interview conditions yields contemporaneous coefficients of 0.089 and 0.067, respectively. The next-wave association is smaller and imprecisely estimated after joint adjustment. The findings link subjective economic position to workers’ evaluations of working conditions.

abstract: We study the effect of expanding patient choice of healthcare provider on care process and clinical outcomes central to the functioning of a health system, using a quasi‐natural experiment in Spain over 2002–2019. Exploiting the staggered adoption of provider choice reforms across Spanish regional health services, we estimate heterogeneity‐robust difference‐in‐differences models on region–year panel data alongside individual‐level survey data. We find that the availability of provider choice reduces specialist waiting times by approximately 17 days (19% of the pre‐reform mean) and the use of private specialist visits, without increasing public health spending. The waiting time and private utilization results are robust to excluding the region where the 2009 reform bundled choice with new hospitals, public–private partnerships, and a budget increase. Although we cannot reject zero effects on some clinical outcomes, the evidence is consistent with the thesis that provider choice improves the ‘quality needle’, namely, it improves observable process quality without affecting less‐visible clinical dimensions.
title: Moving the quality needle? Provider choice, waiting times and clinical outcomes

abstract: Is agricultural productivity conducive to economic development? We develop a two‐country open‐economy Schumpeterian growth model with endogenous takeoff. With both agricultural trade and a subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity has ambiguous effects on the economy's takeoff and its transitional growth rate if domestic and imported agricultural goods are substitutes. Without the subsistence requirement, higher domestic agricultural productivity delays industrialization and lowers transitional growth by increasing domestic demand for agricultural labor. This specialization force works in the opposite direction of the change in domestic consumption pattern governed by the subsistence requirement, which tends to release labor from agriculture. Without agricultural trade, the specialization force is absent and the subsistence requirement on agricultural consumption implies that higher domestic agricultural productivity reallocates labor from agriculture to industry, hastening industrialization and raising transitional growth. Using cross‐country panel data, we find that agricultural productivity has a positive effect on economic growth but this positive effect weakens and even becomes negative when reliance on agricultural imports is sufficiently high. Simulating the calibrated model, we find that improvement in domestic agricultural productivity accounts for about 30% and 15% of the changes in TFP growth in China and Japan, respectively, and more so for their main trading partner, the United States.

abstract: Between 1950 and 2024, world life expectancy increased from below 50 to above 70, while fertility fell from 5 to 2.5. We develop a tractable overlapping-generations climate-economy model and calibrate it to UN demographic projections to study how demographic change affects climate policy through life-cycle savings. The model yields a closed-form social cost of carbon (SCC) in a competitive equilibrium with Pigouvian taxation. Demographic change raises the 2024 SCC from 31.9€/t CO 2 (without demography) to 102.7€/t CO 2 in the calibrated model. The mechanism is positive: lower fertility and longer life expectancy raise aggregate saving and depress equilibrium returns, increasing the present value of a stable climate. The result is robust to a climate–mortality feedback that endogenizes life expectancy, and consistent with cross-country evidence in 176 countries linking the old-to-young dependency ratio to climate policy stringency.
title: Global demographic change and climate policies

abstract: This study tests whether cost-vector design affects welfare estimates from discrete choice experiments (DCEs), and whether repeated choice experience or a pre-DCE open-ended willingness-to-pay (OE WTP) elicitation attenuates that dependence. In a randomized survey of 5,917 Polish adults, respondents valued passive forest protection in Tatra National Park under three cost vectors, two choice-set sizes, and two OE WTP timings. Higher cost vectors consistently produced lower estimated marginal utility of cost and higher WTP. Identical posted prices were also accepted more often in higher-vector contexts, and OE WTP stated after the DCE increased with the vector encountered. Choices became more internally consistent with experience, but WTP still differed across vectors in the last choice tasks. Vector dependence was stable in the two-alternative format and weakened, without disappearing, in the three-alternative format. The pattern survives within-DCE and cross-format consistency exclusions and flexible cost specifications. The evidence rejects context-invariant valuation and shows that greater choice coherence need not imply convergence to context-independent welfare estimates. We recommend multiple cost vectors and pre-specified sensitivity checks in DCE validation.
journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

abstract: In this paper, we study the causal effect of workers’ perceived probability of job loss due to automation on policy preferences and workplace intentions. Using a representative sample of the U.S. workforce, we elicit individuals’ perceived likelihood of losing their job to robots or artificial intelligence within the next decade. We document strong cross-sectional relationships between automation fear and support for higher taxation, more generous government transfers, union membership, retraining, occupational switching, populist attitudes, and voting intentions. To isolate causality, we implement a randomized information treatment that provides occupation-specific job loss probabilities and generates exogenous belief shocks relative to respondents’ own priors. This design is a reduced-form approach to studying how individuals respond to perceived downside exposure to large-scale technological change. Adverse information increases demand for redistribution, government support programs, and unionization. In contrast, it has limited effects on intentions to retrain or switch occupations. Treatment effects are primarily driven by individuals who receive worse news than expected. The asymmetric shifts in expressed preferences to negative belief shocks and the absence of parallel effects on closely related individual margins make a simple social-desirability explanation unlikely. By focusing on perceived employment risk as framed in public discourse, the paper highlights collective protection rather than individual adjustment as the primary margin through which workers might respond to automation risk.
title: The impact of fear of automation

abstract: Married women in the early twentieth-century United States faced “marriage bars,” a form of employer discrimination that barred them from paid employment. However, because the end of marriage bar use coincided with shifting social norms and labor market conditions, it is unclear how the end of marriage bars affected women’s employment. We study the effects of the state-level prohibition of marriage bars in teaching during the 1930s. A difference-in-differences design shows that the prohibitions increased the share of white married women teachers by 4.1 p.p. (26 percent), with no effect on Black teachers.
title: The Effects of Prohibiting Marriage Bars: The Case of U.S. Teachers

abstract: The International Maritime Organisation targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by 2050, considering green ammonia to be a promising fuel for decarbonisation. However, development and deployment of this fuel is contingent not only on aspects such as techno-economic feasibility and supportive policy frameworks, but also on social acceptance (SA). This study examines the community-level SA of a potential green ammonia hub for maritime uses in Ísafjörður, Iceland, a remote coastal settlement with a strong maritime history. Based on sixteen semi-structured interviews with local stakeholders, the study identifies the key drivers and barriers influencing SA. It reveals that perceived benefits such as job creation and environmental protection function as drivers, while barriers stem from perceived concerns regarding safety, cost, and lack of clear governance. Guided by a community-adapted corporate sustainability classification and a PESTLE lens, identified themes are mapped across political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental dimensions. The findings indicate that political and governance conditions function as an important enabling condition for SA, particularly through the perceived need for clear legislative frameworks and government incentives. Rather than operating independently, these political conditions were closely intertwined with economic and technological considerations, influencing investment risk, infrastructure development, affordability, safety, and equitable benefit distribution. The study concludes that for a just maritime energy transition to succeed, national policymakers must prioritise the implementation of robust incentive mechanisms and strategic roadmaps that satisfactorily address local socio-economic realities and contexts.
title: Social acceptance of a green ammonia hub in a remote coastal community – the case of Ísafjörður in Iceland

abstract: This study quantifies how natural disasters affect U.S. food companies and evaluates which diversification strategies mitigate or intensify these effects. We compile a long panel from 1976 to 2023 that links county-level disaster incidence and damages to firm outcomes and supplier–customer relationships in the food sector. The analysis shows that hurricanes are the most consistently economically harmful natural disaster for food processing companies. A firm’s geographical and business structures can mitigate the impact of these shocks. Less customer concentration, more international customer–supplier relationships, and more geographically dispersed branches within the U.S. are all factors associated with smaller effects of hurricanes on aggregate performance. The results are robust to alternative measures of disaster intensity, weighting by firm size, and excluding the COVID-19 period. Overall, the evidence highlights the vulnerability of food production networks to climate-related shocks and informs firm strategy and policy design aimed at strengthening supply-chain resilience.
title: Natural disasters and U.S. food supply chains

abstract: Using CPS data for 1976 to 2025, we explore how wage inequality has evolved for married couples with both spouses working full time full year, and its impact on household income inequality. We also investigate how marriage sorting patterns have changed over this period. To determine the factors driving income inequality we estimate a model explaining the joint distribution of couples’ wages that accounts for spouses’ employment decisions. This requires a multivariate distribution regression model that incorporates a double selection rule. We find that income inequality has increased for these households and increased wage sorting has exacerbated the inequality resulting from individual wage growth. We find that positive sorting partially reflects the correlation across unobservables influencing the wages of both members of the marriage. We decompose the changes in sorting patterns over the 50-year sample into structural, composition and selection effects and find that the increase in positive sorting primarily reflects the increased skill premia for both observed and unobserved characteristics.
title: Marital sorting, household inequality and selection

abstract: This paper investigates the impact of information frictions on trade by leveraging a major historical improvement in news transmission: the rise of global news agencies. Information available to potential traders became more abundant between countries covered by a news agency. Exploiting differences in the timing of telegraph openings and news agency coverage across country pairs, we disentangle the effect of improved information flows from that of reduced communication costs. Panel gravity estimates reveal that bilateral trade increased by 30 percent more for country pairs connected by a news agency and a telegraph than for those connected by a telegraph alone.
title: Information in the First Globalization: News Agencies and Trade

abstract: Cooperation is essential for realizing collective benefits in both small and large groups. Many such interactions are one-shot and differ in the magnitude of collective benefits. Using online public goods games ( N = 2136 ) and two versions of the strategy method, we examine the behavioral structure of cooperation across group sizes (3, 9, and 30) and collective returns (low vs. high). We separately elicit cooperative attitudes — the willingness to contribute conditional on others’ contributions — and beliefs about others’ cooperation. The ABC framework (Attitudes and Beliefs explain Cooperation; Gächter et al. 2017) reveals broadly similar conditionally cooperative attitudes across settings, while higher collective returns are associated with higher beliefs and contributions. Group-size differences in contributions are small. Combining elicited attitudes with beliefs improves out-of-sample predictive accuracy relative to beliefs alone in every environment. These results suggest that the ABC framework provides a parsimonious behavioral foundation for understanding one-shot cooperation.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 252
title: The behavioral structure of one-shot cooperation in small and large groups

abstract: The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective

abstract: We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
title: Housing Yields

abstract: How do incentive levels affect strategic behaviour? We address this with an experiment that separately identifies own- and opponent-incentive effects in two dominance-solvable games that differ in strategic complexity. Higher own incentives favour more strategically sophisticated actions and increase best responding to stated beliefs. Beliefs shift in a parallel direction and participants expect more sophisticated opponent actions. Furthermore, although higher own incentives increase belief accuracy, opponents with higher incentives are harder to predict. Higher incentives also increase response times, and longer response times are associated with better performance and more sophisticated actions and beliefs. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incentives affect strategic behaviour through two main channels: by reducing payoff-dependent mistakes and by increasing the effort devoted to reasoning, with the returns to that effort shaped by strategic complexity of the environment.
title: Incentives and strategic behaviour: an experiment

abstract: We examine the spatial diffusion of housing prices across 152 Chinese cities from 2005 to 2018 through both geographical proximity and socio-economic similarity. We decompose socio-economic similarity into two components: (i) fundamental similarity, measured by similarity in calibrated equilibrium housing prices determined by population, wages, land supply and construction costs; and (ii) non-fundamental similarity, measured by similarity in deviations of observed housing prices from their calibrated equilibrium levels. Using a dynamic spatial panel model, we quantify the magnitude and persistence of housing price shocks. The results show that both geographical and socio-economic diffusion effects are statistically significant and persistent. Neglecting socio-economic linkages may overstate the importance of geographical proximity. Within the socio-economic channel, non-fundamental similarity generates larger and more persistent diffusion effects than fundamental similarity, although fundamental similarity remains an important transmission mechanism. High-tier cities exhibit substantially stronger cross-city diffusion than low-tier cities. Finally, in a leapfrogging subsample that excludes geographically and socio-economically proximate cities, diffusion effects become substantially weaker: non-fundamental effects become statistically insignificant, while fundamental effects remain only weakly significant.

abstract: Using data from the 1997–2015 China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS), this study examines the association between long working hours in young adulthood and health outcomes in middle and older age. The results demonstrate that long working hours in youth are associated with a higher probability of illness in middle and older age. The results remain robust across a series of robustness checks. Channel analyses suggest that reductions in sleep, leisure and exercise and a higher risk of overweight account for part of the observed association. At the same time, longer working hours may be accompanied by economic and subjective resources that provide some offsetting benefits, but these resources are insufficient to fully compensate for the accumulated health costs. Further analyses show that the association is statistically significant in the non-public sector but not in the public sector. Within the non-public sector, it is also statistically significant among rural-hukou workers, men, high-skilled workers and those engaged in light physical work. These patterns suggest that compensation for long working hours may be incomplete across different worker groups. The findings highlight the importance of strengthening working-time regulation, compensation and preventive health protection.

abstract: Singapore’s UNESCO-recognized hawker centres are a compelling case study of government-regulated dining infrastructure offering affordable food to the masses. Today, they face a preservation paradox: how to maintain the social and cultural characteristics that earned them UNESCO heritage status – their form, including open-air settings, communal dining, and locally run stalls – while ensuring the economic viability of the practitioners who operate them and the affordable food they provide – their function. Despite extensive government interventions since the 1970 s, policy responses remain fragmented due to unclear preservation priorities. Without a clear definition of hawker centres as social infrastructure or commercial ventures subject to market forces, the resulting policy ambiguity creates disconnects between stated goals and ground-level realities, sending mixed messages to hawkers about their role and purpose within Singapore’s socioeconomic framework. Little research examines how hawkers themselves respond to these competing expectations. This research examines how hawkers navigate the complex interplay between form and function in policies governing hawker centres and what it reveals about preservation priorities. Twenty-one hawkers across Singapore participated in semi-structured interviews, including both newcomers and multi-generational operators. The analysis examines hawkers’ perspectives on policy impacts, operational challenges, and their vision for the future. Findings reveal three primary disconnects: mandating affordable food despite rising costs; promoting the hawker trade despite declining profitability; and imposing complex regulations while providing minimal market protection. Hawker-generated solutions call for expanding government oversight that treats hawker centres as social infrastructure rather than privatized enterprises. These findings demonstrate that effective cultural heritage preservation requires policy frameworks prioritizing practical functionality over symbolic form, with implications for global food heritage conservation.
title: Who pays for heritage? Examining form-function tensions in Singapore’s hawker centre policies

abstract: In past analyses of animal replacement decisions, studies have claimed that dairy farms often replace dairy cows too early to be maximizing profits. I estimate a structural model of asset replacement to determine the motives behind early replacement of dairy cows. I specifically test whether the costs from premature removal, an event where cows are removed off‐schedule due to health problems, explain replacement ages on dairy farms that are considered by previous studies to be unprofitable. Using data from over 1000 Wisconsin dairy farms, I find that a cow prematurely leaving the herd costs $2300 per removal, totaling $75 million in lost profit over the sample period. This cost is larger than what has been previously assumed, especially for dairies with less than 200 cows, suggesting that replacement rates appear unprofitable because previous analyses underestimated these costs. Dairy farms may benefit from prioritizing cow longevity and health over productivity to both cut costs and address environmental externalities from dairy. These results highlight the economic damages from poor cattle health on US dairy farms and the extent to which there may be cost savings from increasing cattle resilience to conditions that cause unexpected removal.
title: Are dairy cows replaced too early? Evidence from a structural model and cow‐level data

abstract: This study assesses the effects of the 2009 Black Saturday Bushfires (BSB), which primarily occurred in rural regions of Victoria and represent the deadliest bushfire event in Australia's history, on household energy poverty. Using a linear panel event‐study, an entropy‐balanced event‐study, and a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, applied to matched longitudinal household and geographical data, our results suggest a significant increase in the likelihood of experiencing energy poverty among households residing within 15 km of wildfire areas. Specifically, we find that for households directly affected by the fires, the likelihood of being in energy poverty increases by 9.9–11.3 percentage points in 2010 and by 13.2–16.7 percentage points in 2011 across specifications, compared to 2005–2007, which is the reference period. We find that the data are statistically consistent with life satisfaction, perceived safety and quality of life fully mediating the effect of BSB exposure on energy poverty in 2010, and with perceived safety fully mediating the relationship in 2011. We also find that adopting longer‐term financial planning mitigated the adverse effects of BSB exposure on energy poverty.
title: The effect of extreme wildfire exposure on energy poverty: Evidence from Australia's Black Saturday bushfires

abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.
title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation

abstract: Treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates is common in instrumental variable (IV) analyses. An intuitive approach, which we call the interacted two-stage least squares (2sls), is to regress the outcome on the treatment, covariates, and treatment-covariate interactions, using the IV, covariates, and IV-covariate interactions as instruments. We clarify the causal interpretation of the interacted 2sls under the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework when the IV is valid conditional on the covariates. Our main findings are twofold. First, we show that the coefficients on the treatment-covariate interactions from the interacted 2sls identify treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates among compliers for any outcome-generating process if and only if the product of the IV propensity score and the covariates is linear in the covariates, a requirement we call the linear IV-covariate interactions condition. Second, when the covariate vector has dimension K and includes a constant term, we show that the linear IV-covariate interactions condition requires the IV propensity score to take at most K distinct values. The condition holds when (a) the covariates take exactly K distinct values, or (b) the IV is randomly assigned independently of the covariates, but is restrictive beyond these cases. These results underscore the difficulty of interpreting regression coefficients from specifications with treatment-covariate interactions when the covariates are not saturated and the IV is not unconditionally randomized, absent correct specification of the outcome model. We then connect these results to the literature on LATE estimation, and show that under the linear IV-covariate interactions condition, the interacted 2sls with covariates demeaned by their complier means recovers the LATE as a single coefficient.
title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity

abstract: Bankers may benefit from the upside of risk-taking through bonuses, while taxpayers may ultimately bear the costs when things go badly wrong. After the Global Financial Crisis, regulators set out to change how bank executives are paid. This column examines how compensation practices have evolved since then and how they relate to bank risk. Longer deferral horizons, as mandated in the EU, have reduced bank risk-taking, but evidence on bonus caps is inconclusive. The 2023 banking turmoil shows that bank boards and supervisors play a crucial role in ensuring good governance of compensation frameworks.
authors: Gaston Gelos, Bertrand Rime, Kevin Tracol
title: Bank executive pay: Compensation design can help reduce excessive risk-taking

abstract: From employer wage-setting power to the consequences of pay transparency and the role of benefits in compensation inequality, many core questions about labour markets hinge on how job seekers respond to wage and benefit differences across job ads. Combining a field experiment on over 100 Swiss job boards with a survey, this column shows that workers are imperfectly informed about wage and benefit differences across jobs. Posting wages redirects search towards better-paying jobs. Workers also value certain benefits highly – notably company cars and the option to work from home. Since higher-paying jobs tend to offer more benefits, inequality in job value exceeds wage inequality across jobs.
authors: Andreas Beerli, Stefano Fiorin, Andreas Gulyas, Daniel Kopp, Mahsa Khoshnama, Michael Siegenthaler
title: Job seekers’ beliefs and preferences over wages and benefits: Experimental evidence from online job boards

abstract: Misperceptions of others’ concern about climate change have been identified as key barriers to climate action. We study whether people also misperceive (i) others’ level of sustainable behavior, (ii) the level of sustainable behavior others deem appropriate, and (iii) others’ support for policies that restrict or tax individual non-sustainable behavior. We address these questions in a pre-registered online study with 1292 Luxembourg residents. Participants reported their own behaviors, personal norms, and policy support, and estimated the same for others across three domains with high carbon-saving potential: reducing animal protein consumption, reducing home heating, and using public transportation. In line with pluralistic ignorance, we find that a majority of participants systematically and substantially underestimate others’ sustainability. Participants also underestimate how much others donate to offset carbon emissions in an incentivized donation task. Consistent with a false consensus effect, the least sustainable individuals strongly underestimate others’ sustainability, while the most sustainable underestimate less and even overestimate in some domains.
title: Society might be greener than you think

abstract: The World Bank uses a population threshold of 1.5 million as the operational reference point for its Small States classification, with implications across several financing frameworks. This paper asks whether there is a break at the threshold in the macroeconomic outcomes associated with small country size, and how the classification rule should be administered given that population estimates are revised. In cross-country data for emerging market and developing economies over 2000–24, growth volatility, trade openness, and terms-of-trade volatility decline smoothly with population size across regression, nonparametric, and threshold-test evidence, with no detectable break at 1.5 million or at any alternative cutoff between 1 and 10 million. In a newly assembled real-time data set of 15 annual vintages, half of the published population estimates are revised by more than 1 percent within five years, and an estimate that is 1 percent above the threshold faces roughly a one-in-four probability of being revised below it within five years. Of the three Small State status changes since 2019, two resulted from revisions, not demographic change. Within the existing threshold-based framework, the paper evaluates four implementation rules, including the current single-year rule, and recommends an asymmetric persistence requirement—immediate entry and exit only after three consecutive years above the threshold—supplemented by an advance-notice flag based on estimated crossing probabilities.
journal: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
publisher: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
series: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
source_name: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
title: Population Thresholds and Classification Stability: Evidence from the World Bank’s Small States Classification Rule

abstract: Background. We aim to quantify changes in the percentage of US citizens suffering extreme distress since 1993. Methods. Using data on 10.9 million randomly sampled US citizens between 1993 and 2024, we present raw and covariate-adjusted trends in the incidence of extreme distress defined as the percentage who report major mental and emotional problems in all 30 of the last 30 days. We present trends for men and women separately and distinguish between the young and the old, and by work status. Results. Extreme distress has almost doubled since 1993. It rose for men and women, workers and non-workers. But the biggest increases were among young workers – particularly women.
title: Trends in extreme distress in the United States, 1993–2024

abstract: A challenge in sustainable tourism development is whether tourism-oriented conservation policies can simultaneously achieve environmental protection and local employment transformation. This study provides causal evidence by leveraging the designation of China’s National Scenic and Historic Interest Areas (NSHIAs) as a quasi-natural experiment. Employing panel data for 195 Chinese cities from 2000 to 2022 and a multi-period difference-in-differences approach, we estimate the effects of NSHIA designation on environmental quality and employment transformation. The results show that the establishment of NSHIAs significantly improves environmental quality while increasing service-sector employment. Further analysis reveals significant spatial spillover effects, with improvements in environmental conditions and service-sector employment extending to neighbouring cities. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that these effects are more pronounced in cities with higher tourism dependence and in areas that are also designated as World Heritage sites. Overall, tourism-oriented conservation policies can simultaneously yield environmental and socioeconomic benefits, with implications for balancing conservation and development.
china_relevance_reason: 标题、摘要或元数据包含中国相关关键词
title: The environmental and employment effects of tourism-oriented conservation policies: evidence from China’s National Scenic and Historic Interest Areas

abstract: This article examines how stated support for renewable electricity financing and stated willingness to adopt residential solar photovoltaic (PV) systems respond to experimentally varied prices, subsidies, and expected bill savings in Mexico, a country with vast solar potential but distorted electricity markets. Using randomized survey experiments, we analyze support for financing utility-scale renewables through electricity bill surcharges and stated responses to alternative residential solar incentive schemes. The results reveal a “green support gap”: support for renewable expansion declines substantially when it is framed as increasing household electricity bills. Regarding residential solar adoption, we find sub-additivity between upfront subsidies and expected bill savings, an effect that is weaker among lower-income households, consistent with the possibility that affordability constraints influence how financial incentives are evaluated. Furthermore, we find that realized bill savings reported by adopters are 152% higher than the expectations reported by non-adopters. This pattern is consistent with pessimistic beliefs regarding private financial returns to solar investment, which act as a key barrier preventing general interest in the technology from translating into near-term adoption choices and realized ownership. Overall, the results provide evidence on how households evaluate alternative financing and incentive frames for clean energy investment in an emerging economy facing fiscal and climate policy trade-offs.
title: Who pays for clean power? Evidence on public support and solar adoption intentions in Mexico

abstract: Does social protection at home make workers less likely to plan to leave? Using the nationally representative 2021 Tunisia Household International Migration Survey, we compare 4228 non-migrants employed before COVID-19 and covered by contributory social insurance, by state assistance, or by neither. Inverse probability weighted regression adjustment with survey weights indicates that contributory workers are 7.1 percentage points less likely to intend to migrate than comparable unprotected workers, against a counterfactual rate of 23.3%. For recipients of state assistance, the gap is 6.1 points, less precise and less robust, and concentrated outside Grand Tunis, among single people and among temporary employees. Both regimes are associated with a lower probability of planning to leave within a year. Each regime combines protection with a position in the labour market, so the estimates describe regime membership and not the effect of specific benefits. Extending contributory coverage to informal workers is the policy option most consistent with these findings.
title: Origin-country social protection regimes and migration intentions: Evidence from Tunisia

abstract: Using data from 1,077 unique firms operating in 16 developing countries from 2007 to 2021, this paper examines how social capital influences corporate corruption. While the bright side of social capital encourages collective action, the dark side promotes impunity and groupthink, disregarding moral considerations. We test these alternative outcomes and find that the dark side of social capital is more prevalent in developing countries. The positive association between social capital and corruption is stronger for firms facing high market competition and cash holding, and during periods of uncertainty and geopolitical risk. However, social capital plays a disciplinary role for firms seeking legitimacy while going through operational internalization. Our results remain robust after controlling for endogeneity and employing alternative estimation strategies. Overall, the findings show that in developing countries, strong social networks and informal relationships enable firms to use corruption as a means to navigate institutional constraints and bureaucratic inefficiencies.
title: Unveiling the Dark Side: The Role of Social Capital in Corporate Corruption in Developing Countries

abstract: We study the design and pricing of information by independent information providers for a buyer engaged in a trading relationship with a seller, and examine their welfare implications. While competitive information firms would sell full information about the value of the good, a monopolist supplies limited information in a particularly simple form—often resulting in higher total surplus than under full information, by influencing the seller's pricing decision. If only a single information structure can be offered, it takes a binary threshold form. If the provider can offer a menu of priced information structures before the seller sets a price, he offers a continuum of thresholds, inducing a unit‐elastic demand function for the seller. In both scenarios, the information firm increases total welfare when the seller's production cost is high but reduces it when the cost is low.
title: Selling information for bilateral trade
title_zh: 双边贸易中的信息出售

abstract: We consider a privately informed principal selecting a communication device to influence players' actions. In contrast to standard information design, the principal cannot commit ex ante, and the device must elicit information from all players. We define an informed communication equilibrium (informed CE) as a perfect Bayesian equilibrium outcome of this informed communication design game. We show that the set of informed CE is the subset of communication equilibria (CE) that yield principal payoff vectors bounded below by an equilibrium payoff vector of the silent game, under some consistent interim beliefs. The ex ante optimal CE may fail to be an informed CE. We provide sufficient conditions for a CE to be an informed CE and identify classes of games in which CE and informed CE coincide.
title: Informed communication equilibrium

abstract: We study the ability of multigroup teams to undertake binary projects in a decentralized environment. The equilibrium outcomes of our model display familiar features in collaborative settings, including inefficient gradualism, inaction, and contribution cycles, wherein groups alternate taking responsibility for moving the project forward. Expected delay grows more than proportionally with project size, and some welfare‐enhancing projects are not completed, even as agents become arbitrarily patient. A team composed of two equally large groups can complete larger projects than a fully homogeneous team, even as the difference in preferences for completion among the two groups is arbitrarily small. Moreover, if the project is sufficiently large, the two‐group team always completes the project strictly faster.
title: Collaboration between and within groups
title_zh: 群体内与群体间的协作

abstract: In complex strategic settings with multiple dimensions, players often simplify decisions by breaking them down into separate dimensions. In contrast to standard replicator dynamics, which assume perfect multidimensional coordination, our combinator dynamics model captures cases in which players revise actions dimension by dimension, imitate successful traits in each dimension, and then combine the selected traits into a new action. We analyze key properties of these dynamics—monotonicity, stationarity, and stability. We then extend the model to heterogeneous settings, where some players imitate entire multidimensional actions while others combine traits imitated separately in each dimension. We apply the framework to organizational decision‐making, where decentralized adoption of practices can generate coordination failures, persistent performance differences, and a trade‐off between specialized and versatile organizational traits.
title: Combinator dynamics: Multidimensional evolutionary learning

abstract: We study the roommate problem allowing for preferences with indifferences and agents remaining single. A stable outcome need not exist. We introduce semi‐stability, a novel notion that guarantees existence and restores stability through minimal policy or group interventions. We build an equilibrium foundation for semistability by showing its equivalence to a newly proposed choice‐based equilibrium concept. We show that undominated semistable outcomes are Pareto optimal and under strict preferences, every semistable outcome is Pareto optimal. Nevertheless, standard structural properties, such as the rural hospital theorem and the lattice properties, fail for semistable outcomes. We also discuss possible applications.
title: Semistability in roommate problems

abstract: We study doctor–hospital matching markets with contracts, in which hospitals can offer a range of contract terms to doctors. We show that introducing new terms can reduce doctors' welfare, whereas withdrawing terms may generate a Pareto improvement. We establish the preference domains under which welfare is preserved and show that only agent‐lexicographic preferences for all agents ensure that no doctor is worse off when additional terms are introduced. Since this condition is rarely satisfied in practice, our results imply that most real‐world markets are vulnerable to welfare losses when the set of contract terms expands.
title: Contract terms monotonicity in matching markets
title_zh: 匹配市场中的合同条款单调性

abstract: We study the design of an auction for an income‐generating asset such as an intellectual property license. Each bidder has a signal about his future income from acquiring the asset. After the asset is allocated, the winner's income from the asset is realized privately. The principal can audit the winner, at a cost, and then charge a payment contingent on the winner's realized income. We solve for an auction that maximizes the principal's revenue, net of auditing costs. The winning bidder is charged linear royalties up to a cap, beyond which there is no auditing. A higher bidder pays more in cash upfront and faces a lower royalty cap.
title: Optimal auction design with contingent payments and costly verification
title_zh: 带有条件支付和昂贵验证的最优拍卖设计

abstract: We study information design in games where players choose from a continuum of actions and have continuously differentiable payoffs. We show that an information structure is optimal when the equilibrium it induces can also be implemented in a principal–agent contracting problem. Building on this result, we characterize optimal information structures in symmetric linear‐quadratic games. With common values, targeted disclosure is robustly optimal across all priors. With interdependent and normally distributed values, linear disclosure is uniquely optimal. We illustrate our findings with applications in venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.
title: Information design in smooth games
title_zh: 平滑博弈中的信息设计

abstract: Motivated by the problem of sustaining cooperation in large groups with limited information, we analyze the relationship between group size, monitoring precision, and discounting in repeated games with independent, player‐level noise. The viability of cooperation under independent noise is linked to the per‐capita channel capacity of the stage‐game monitoring structure. We show that cooperation is impossible if the per‐capita channel capacity is much smaller than the discount rate. A folk theorem under a novel identification condition provides a near converse. If attention is restricted to co‐linear equilibria (a generalization of strongly symmetric equilibria), cooperation is possible only under much more severe parameter restrictions.
title: Repeated games with many players

abstract: Studies find that people systematically underestimate the likelihood of streaks in a random sequence. In a canonical coin‐tossing environment, this paper shows that the evidence can be explained by a belief in mean reversion. Such beliefs are represented as if the bias of the coin is history‐dependent and “self‐correcting.” In a Bayesian inference setting, a belief in mean reversion ensures that the agent never rules out the true parameter.
title: Belief in mean reversion and the law of small numbers
title_zh: 均值回归信念与小数字定律

abstract: We study a strategic experimentation game with exponential bandits in which experiment outcomes are private. The equilibrium amount of experimentation is always weakly higher than with public outcomes. Moreover, in pure equilibria, experimentation is never significantly below the socially optimal level and may be strictly higher. We provide a tight bound on the extent of over‐experimentation. The analysis rests on a novel encouragement effect.
title: Strategic experimentation with privately observed payoffs
title_zh: 私有收益下的策略性实验

abstract: In July 2022 the ten-digit National Suicide Prevention Lifeline was replaced with a dedicated three-digit number, 988. This followed a precipitous rise in the suicide rate, especially among youth. Suicide is now the second leading cause of death among Americans aged 15 to 24. In this paper, I estimate the effect of 988 on youth and overall suicide rates. I show that the rollout of 988 increased the number of calls to suicide hotlines and the share of calls that were answered. Nonetheless, I find no evidence that 988 reduced suicide mortality. Using multiple identification strategies, I find no reduction following the national rollout in July 2022, nor do I find evidence that state-level improvements in call answer rates reduced suicide. These findings do not imply that 988 has been ineffective: the rollout clearly improved hotline access and response rates. However, I find no evidence that it reduced emergency-department visits for injuries caused by self-harm.
title: The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and Youth Suicide

abstract: Workers care not only about pay and career opportunities but also about meaningful work and socially responsible employers. This heterogeneity matters for worker-firm matching, recruitment, and compensation, yet its preference-based origins remain poorly understood. Using a two-wave study representative of the Swiss population (N=1,031), we study whether social preferences account for life goals, job preferences, and occupational sorting. We structurally estimate two facets of social preferences: altruism in the advantageous and disadvantageous domains. These dimensions are negatively correlated; failing to account for both substantially underestimates the effects of social preferences. Social preferences predict life goals, preferred job attributes, and willingness to work in the tobacco industry. Higher altruism is associated with a lower emphasis on wealth, career status, and pay, but a greater emphasis on corporate social responsibility and meaningful work. Lastly, altruism when ahead positively associates with employment in education, health, and social services. Our paper highlights the importance of social preferences for worker motivation and labor-market sorting.
title: The Role of Social Preferences for Life Goals and Career Choices
